extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of media, public opinion, and political theory; general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for how popular representation (news, fiction, motion pictures, propaganda) must be constructed to engage audiences and shape public opinion; includes norms about visualization, identification, suspense, stereotypes, and the role of self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization / Pictorial Faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and next in order, words that call up pictures in memory."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear thinkers are often good visualizers; visualization gives ideas visual/tactile value necessary for practical decision. But visualizers may caricature the intermediate and internal life that intuition (musical/muscular perception) perceives. Effective media should translate ideas into recognizable images that confer practical value and permit identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification (Empathy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The idea conveyed is not fully our own until we have identified ourselves with some aspect of the picture. The identification, or what Vernon Lee has called empathy... may be almost infinitely subtle and symbolic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification can be explicit (popular representations mark the hero clearly) or subtle (symbolic empathy). Popular works that fail to provide handles for identification will not easily be popular. Identification is necessary for audience engagement and for a work to 'be ours.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Must Be Exercised / Active Engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: "The audience must have something to do, and the contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do. In order not to sit inertly... the audience must be exercised by the image."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid passive spectatorship, content must invite action or emotional involvement (taking sides, suspense, rooting for outcome). Works that merely present contemplative beauty without activating drives will fail to hold mass attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Drives for Mass Appeal: Sexual Passion and Fighting
rubrics_metrics.description: "They are sexual passion and fighting, and the two have so many associations with each other... that a fight about sex outranks every other theme in the breadth of its appeal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual and combative motifs are the easiest and most eager stimuli for broad audiences; mass entertainment routinely exploits these motifs to arouse interest. Absence of these motifs reduces mass appeal except in niche contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pugnacity/Issue-Driven Interest in Politics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Politics is interesting when there is a fight, or as we say, an issue. And in order to make politics popular, issues have to be found, even when in truth and justice, there are none..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political narratives are made engaging by framing disputes as fights/issues; producers may manufacture or emphasize issues to enlist pugnacity and sustain public attention, even if substantive differences are minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense as Central Engagement Mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: "suspense... constitutes the difference between the masterpieces in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the pictures at the Rivoli or the Rialto Theatres."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion pictures and popular narratives hold attention through unfolding events and struggle; suspense derived from an unresolved conflict or obstacle keeps audiences longer and is a key device for mass appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability of Distant/Abstract Situations into Recognizable Pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: "In order then that the distant situation shall not be a gray flicker on the edge of attention, it should be capable of translation into pictures in which the opportunity for identification is recognizable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract or remote public affairs must be rendered into concrete, picturable scenes that invite identification; otherwise they will interest only a few people for a short time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic Beginning and Romantic (Desirable) Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our popular taste is to have the drama originate in a setting realistic enough to make identification plausible and to have it terminate in a setting romantic enough to be desirable... the true beginning and the happy ending are landmarks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular narratives should anchor the audience with plausible, familiar openings and promise a desirable, preferably happy, resolution; pure fantasy or relentless realism tends to lose broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to and Constraints of Stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: "The men who make moving pictures... must adhere to the stereotypes that they find, or pay the price of frustrating expectation. The stereotypes can be altered, but not in time to guarantee success when the film is released six months from now."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic and production constraints push creators to use existing stereotypes because quickly altering public perceptions risks commercial failure. Innovators may change stereotypes but face commercial resistance; successful innovations themselves become new stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Pioneering Artists versus Commercial Managers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The men who do alter the stereotypes, the pioneering artists and critics, are naturally depressed and angered at managers and editors who protect their investments... They are asking for circulations and audiences that were never considered by any artist until the last few generations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a tension between artistic innovation (which seeks to expand repertory of images) and commercial managers (who protect investments by relying on proven stereotypes); evaluation must consider commercial constraints and differing success metrics (circulation vs. aesthetic value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of Story Reception by Audience Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The identical story is not the same story to all who hear it. Each will enter it at a slightly different point... The original theme as it circulates, is stressed, twisted, and embroidered by all the minds through which it goes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As audience heterogeneity increases, responses diverge and common factors in a story become more abstract; communicators should anticipate multiple interpretations and the tendency of stories to be reshaped in circulation (rumor, gossip effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Which 'Self' Is Engaged Determines Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is of great importance in the formation of any public opinion, what self is engaged... whether you conceive the demand as a desire to grow fruit or to marry the white man's daughter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals possess multiple selves (roles/personas) that can be activated by context; persuasive messaging and reporting must consider which self (economic actor, family head, patriot, etc.) will be evoked because that determines emotional intensity and stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Consistency and Variability in Public Behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no one self always at work... People differ widely... If the selves are too unrelated, we distrust the man; if they are too inflexibly on one track we find him arid, stubborn, or eccentric."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should recognize that individuals display different characters in different contexts; appeals that ignore this variability risk mischaracterizing public reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Education Should Prepare People for Realistic Modern Situations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The preparation of characters for all the situations in which men may find themselves is one function of a moral education... Either he must abolish war, or teach people how to wage it with the greatest psychic economy..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative frameworks (moral education, institutions) that fail to address modern complexities leave people unprepared; creators of public messaging or policy education should offer practical patterns of conduct for likely real-world dilemmas rather than idealized prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Component of Self-Interest; Critique of Economic Determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ordinary doctrine of self-interest usually omits altogether the cognitive function... men's ideas of all things and of themselves are not instinctive. They are acquired... economic determinist cannot tell."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses that assume economic position deterministically determines opinion are flawed; opinion formation involves cognition, interpretation, and multiple social relations. Predictive claims based solely on economic class are unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagandist Narrative Formula: Plausible Analysis then Utopian Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: "The skilful propagandist knows that while you must start with a plausible analysis, you must not keep on analyzing... the propagandist exhausts the interest in reality by a tolerably plausible beginning, and then stokes up energy for a long voyage by brandishing a passport to heaven."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda and ideology work by anchoring in plausible present grievances and then offering a comforting or glorious future; evaluators should be alert to this rhetorical structure and its manipulative potency.
